name: Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit
definition: Leaders are obligated to respectfully challenge decisions when they disagree, even when doing so is uncomfortable or exhausting. Leaders have conviction and are tenacious. They do not compromise for the sake of social cohesion. Once a decision is determined, they commit wholly.

rows.situation: When you disagree in the meeting
rows.under: Disagrees privately and stays quiet if nobody else speaks. The room never hears the other view.
rows.justRight: Offers an alternative, names the flaws and benefits of each path, and asks for the follow-up if more data is required.
rows.over: Lists the flaws and never proposes another way forward.

rows.under: Sits quietly despite having data that cuts against the popular position, then nods once the decision is made.
rows.justRight: Disagrees with peers and with people above them, using data. Once the decision is made, works to make it succeed, and still raises an unaddressed fact if one appears.
rows.over: States the counter-position with heat and no facts. Takes offense. After the decision, withholds support and keeps criticizing.

rows.situation: When the first room did not move
rows.under: Nods at the boss, then complains in the hallway.
rows.justRight: Makes the case, loses, and escalates once with relevant data. Does not turn the escalation into a campaign.
rows.over: Tells everyone the group is making a mistake, builds an emotional case, and hopes the work fails.

rows.situation: When the evidence starts to move
rows.under: Never states a point of view. Agrees too fast and does not test the other side.
rows.justRight: Advocates clearly and with conviction, then fully commits to the outcome once the decision is made, including when the evidence changed their mind.
rows.over: Sticks to the original opinion after better evidence arrives, and sabotages the final call.

rows.under: Will not engage. Suffers in silence.
rows.justRight: Debates the issue, not the person. Knows when to agree, then sells the decision as if it were their own.
rows.over: Too argumentative to support a consensus, even after the call is made.

rows.situation: When the room needs to hear you
rows.under: Style is weak and without conviction. Nobody buys in, because the speaker does not seem to care.
rows.justRight: Is direct, invites the other views, and keeps the discussion about the customer and the long term.
rows.over: Style is so aggressive that other people stop sharing. The loudest voice wins, and the data leaves the room.

rows.situation: When the decision did not go your way
rows.under: Completes the work they disagree with and stays silent. No energy, and no honest commit.
rows.justRight: Supports the group decision as if it were their own. Knows when to move on. Brings a new fact if the world changes.
rows.over: Argues their point after the decision, or works at half speed so they can say they were right later.

rows.under: Splits the difference so nobody is wrong. The customer gets the worse outcome.
rows.justRight: Gets the tape measure. Holds the uncomfortable fact in the room until the decision is actually better.
rows.over: Delays the decision so they can keep talking. Debates to look smart, not to improve the call.

rows.situation: When the committed path is failing
rows.under: Leaves the failing path in place and suffers through it.
rows.justRight: Meets the original proponent, reviews the evidence, and agrees the next step. Does not use the miss as a chance to say I told you so.
rows.over: Presents the failure in public as proof the original direction was foolish.

rows.situation: When you have to carry a decision to your team
rows.under: Tells the team you were overruled, so they inherit your opposition.
rows.justRight: Presents the decision as the team's decision, walks through the alternatives that lost, and lines people up to make it true.
rows.over: Sells a fake enthusiasm nobody believes, or refuses to explain the reasoning at all.
